summary: Lists requirements for the TCP/IP header compression scheme to be developed by the Robust Header Compression working group. It discusses scope, performance, assumptions about the environment, and intellectual-property concerns. Its structure comes from RFC 3096. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4163 is a list of what a TCP header compression scheme has to achieve if it is to work on the kind of links where packets get lost and take a long time to arrive. It also has to work with the header compression framework already in use, and it has to leave the rest of the network untouched.

questions: why compress tcp headers on cellular links
what does rohc tcp have to compress
why must a compression scheme leave the tcp checksum alone
subtitle: What a TCP header compression scheme has to do before it can be called robust.

tldr.problem: TCP has always run over reliable links, so the existing header compression schemes were never built to survive a lossy radio link, and no scheme existed that could efficiently compress modern TCP headers with options such as SACK and ECN.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists the requirements in five groups: what a compression scheme must not break, which headers it must handle, how well it must perform, what the link underneath it may do, and the intellectual property position it has to be in.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo of requirements only. The scheme itself is to be developed by the Robust Header Compression working group, and the memo adds no security risk of its own.

today: RFC 4163 is an Informational memo published in August 2005, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It states the requirements for the TCP profile of the Robust Header Compression framework, whose general framework and other profiles are defined in RFC 3095.

sections.title: Why TCP Header Compression
sections.content:
The goal of the ROHC working group is to develop header compression schemes that perform well over links with high error rates and long link roundtrip times. The schemes must perform well for cellular links that use technologies such as Wideband Code Division Multiple Access, Enhanced Data rates for GSM Evolution and CDMA2000, while also being applicable to other link technologies with high loss and long roundtrip times.

The main objective for ROHC has been robust compression of IP, UDP and RTP, but the working group is also chartered to develop new header compression solutions for IP over TCP. Because TCP traffic, in contrast to RTP, has usually been sent over reliable links, existing schemes for TCP have not experienced the same robustness problems as RTP compression. There are still many scenarios where TCP header compression will be implemented over less reliable links, which makes robustness an important objective for the new TCP compression scheme.

The other objectives for ROHC TCP compression are improved compression efficiency, enhanced capabilities for compression of header fields including TCP options, and finally incorporation of TCP compression into the ROHC framework.
sections.plainLanguage: Compressing a TCP header is worth doing on a slow radio link, because the header is a fixed cost on every packet. The catch is that on a bad link packets are lost and arrive out of order, and a compression scheme that cannot cope with that will corrupt the stream. That is the hard part this memo is about.

sections.title: Impact on the Internet Infrastructure
sections.content:
Two requirements govern the effect of a header compression scheme on the rest of the Internet infrastructure.

Transparency. When a header is compressed and then decompressed, the resulting header must be semantically identical to the original header. If this cannot be achieved, the packet containing the erroneous header must be discarded. The justification given is that the header compression process must not produce headers that might cause problems for any current or future part of the Internet infrastructure. The memo adds a note: the working group has not found a case where semantically identical is not the same as bitwise identical.

Ubiquity. The scheme must not require modifications to existing IP, whether version 4 or version 6, or TCP implementations. The justification is ease of deployment. The memo adds two notes. The working group may recommend changes that would increase the compression efficiency for the TCP streams emitted by implementations, but ROHC cannot assume such recommendations will be followed. And several TCP variants are currently in use on the Internet, so the scheme must work efficiently and correctly for all expected TCP variants.
sections.plainLanguage: Two rules. The header that comes out at the far end has to be the same header that went in, or the packet is thrown away. And nothing else in the network may have to be changed to make the scheme work, because a scheme that needs changes everywhere will not be deployed anywhere.

sections.title: Which Headers Must Be Compressed
sections.content:
The second group defines what kind of headers must be compressed efficiently.

IPv4 and IPv6. The scheme must support both. All expected changes in the IP header fields must be handled, and commonly changing fields should be compressed efficiently. Compression must still be possible when IPv6 extensions are present in the header. When designing the scheme, the usage of Explicit Congestion Notification should be considered as a common behavior, so the scheme must also compress efficiently when the ECN bits are used. The justification is that IPv4 and IPv6 will both be around for the foreseeable future, that options and extensions are expected to become more commonly used, and that ECN is expected to have a breakthrough and be widely deployed, especially in combination with TCP.

Mobile IP. The kinds of headers used by Mobile IP for IPv4 and IPv6 must be supported and should be compressed efficiently. For IPv4 these include headers of tunneled packets; for IPv6 they include headers containing the Routing Header and the Home Address Option. The justification is that Mobile IP is very likely to be used by cellular devices.

Generality. The scheme must handle all headers from arbitrary TCP streams. There must be a generic scheme that can compress reasonably well for any TCP traffic pattern, though this does not preclude optimizations for certain traffic patterns.

IPsec. The scheme should be able to compress headers containing IPsec subheaders where the NULL encryption algorithm is used, because IPsec is expected to be used to provide necessary end-to-end security. The memo notes that it is not possible to compress the encrypted part of an ESP header, nor the cryptographic data in an AH header.

TCP. All fields supported by RFC 2507 should be handled with efficient compression, as should the cases when the SYN, FIN or TCP ECN bits are set, because these bits are expected to be commonly used.

TCP options. The scheme must support compression of packets with any TCP option present, even if the option itself is not compressed. For some commonly used options the scheme should also provide compression mechanisms for the options. The justification is that various TCP options are commonly used, and the applicability of the scheme would be significantly reduced if packets with options could not be compressed. The options that should be compressed are Selective Acknowledgement and Timestamp.
sections.plainLanguage: The scheme has to cope with everything that can appear in an IP or TCP header, including the optional parts: IPv6 extension headers, the congestion notification bits, the tunnel headers that Mobile IP adds, and any TCP option a program might turn on. It has to work on traffic it has never seen before, not just on the patterns the designers thought of.

sections.title: Performance Requirements
sections.content:
Performance and spectral efficiency. The scheme must provide low relative overhead under expected operating conditions, and compression efficiency should be better than for RFC 2507 under equivalent operating conditions. Spectrum efficiency is a primary goal. The note defines the relative overhead as the average header overhead relative to the payload, and says that any auxiliary channels used by the scheme, for example control or feedback channels, should be taken into account when calculating the header overhead.

Losses between compressor and decompressor. The scheme should make sure that losses between the compressor and the decompressor do not result in losses of subsequent packets, and do not cause damage to the context that results in incorrect decompression of subsequent packet headers. Even though link layer retransmission is in most cases expected to almost eliminate such losses, there are still many scenarios where TCP header compression will be implemented over less reliable links, and in such cases loss propagation due to header compression could affect certain TCP mechanisms that are capable of handling some losses, and could also have a negative impact on the performance of TCP loss recovery.

Residual errors in compressed headers. Residual errors may result in delivery of incorrectly decompressed headers not only for the damaged packet itself, but also for subsequent packets, because errors may be saved in the context state. For TCP the compression scheme is not required to implement explicit mechanisms for residual error detection, but it must not affect TCP's end-to-end mechanisms for error detection. The note says this requirement implies that the TCP checksum must be carried unmodified in all compressed headers, and that the error detection mechanism in TCP may be able to detect residual bit errors, but that the mechanism is not designed for this purpose and might provide rather weak protection, so although it is not a requirement of the scheme it should be possible for the decompressor to detect residual errors and discard such packets.

Short-lived TCP transfers. The scheme should provide mechanisms for efficient compression of short-lived TCP transfers, minimizing the size of context initiation headers. Many TCP transfers are short-lived, which may lead to a low gain for schemes that, for each new packet stream, require full headers to be sent initially and allow small compressed headers only after the initialization phase. The note says this implies that mechanisms for building new contexts that are based on information from previous contexts, or for concurrent packet streams to share context information, should be considered.

Misordering. The scheme should efficiently handle moderate misordering, that is 2 to 3 packets, in the packet stream reaching the compressor, because this kind of misordering is common. It must be able to correctly handle packet misordering, and preferably compress when misordered packets are in the TCP stream reaching the compressor, because misordering happens regularly in the Internet. However, because the Internet is engineered to run TCP reasonably well, excessive misordering will not be common and need not be handled with optimum efficiency.

Processing delay. The scheme should not contribute significantly to the system delay budget.
sections.plainLanguage: The scheme has to save more space than the older one did, and it must not make a lost packet take the rest of the stream down with it. Two details matter for TCP in particular: the checksum must be left exactly as it was, so that TCP's own error detection still works, and the first few packets of a short connection must be cheap, because short connections are the common case on a radio link.

sections.title: Requirements From the Link Layer and on Patents
sections.content:
Unidirectional links. It must be possible to implement the scheme, possibly with less efficiency, without explicit feedback messages from the decompressor to the compressor. There are links that do not provide a feedback channel, or where feedback is not desirable for other reasons.

Link delay. The scheme must operate under all expected link delay conditions.

Header compression coexistence. The scheme must fit into the ROHC framework together with other ROHC profiles.

Misordering between compressor and decompressor. When compression is applied over tunnels, misordering often cannot be completely avoided. The header compression scheme should not prohibit misordering between the compressor and the decompressor, as it would therefore not be applicable in many tunnelling scenarios. However, in the case of tunnelling it is usually possible to get misordering indications, so the compression scheme does not have to support detection of misordering, but can assume that such information is available from lower layers when misordering occurs.

Intellectual Property Rights. The ROHC working group must spend effort to achieve a high degree of confidence that there are no known IPR claims that cover the final compression solution for TCP. The justification is that currently there is no TCP header compression scheme available that can efficiently compress the packet headers of modern TCP, for example with SACK and ECN, so ROHC is expected to fill this gap by providing a ROHC TCP scheme that is applicable in the wide area Internet, not only over error-prone radio links. It must therefore attempt to be as future-proof as possible, and only unencumbered solutions, or solutions where the terms of any IPR are such that there is no hindrance on implementation and deployment, will be acceptable to the Internet at large.
sections.plainLanguage: The link underneath may be slow, may not be able to send anything back, and may deliver packets in the wrong order, and the scheme still has to work. On patents the memo is blunt: the working group has to be confident that nothing in the final scheme is covered by someone else's claim, because a scheme nobody can implement freely is worth nothing to the Internet.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
A protocol specified to meet these requirements must be able to compress packets containing IPsec headers according to the IPsec requirement in section 2.2. There may be other security aspects to consider in such protocols, but this document by itself does not add any security risks.

On IANA, the memo notes that a protocol meeting these requirements will require IANA to assign various numbers, but that the document by itself does not require any IANA involvement.
sections.plainLanguage: The document adds no risk of its own. The only security point is that a scheme meeting these requirements still has to be able to compress IPsec headers where the null encryption algorithm is used, because otherwise the security would have to be given up.

viz.caption: THE OBJECTIVES FOR ROHC TCP COMPRESSION

items.title: High error rates
items.text: The scheme must perform well over links with high error rates, and losses between the compressor and decompressor must not destroy the packets that follow.

items.title: Long roundtrip times
items.text: It must perform well over links with long link roundtrip times, and must operate under all expected link delay conditions.

items.title: Better compression
items.text: Compression efficiency should be better than for RFC 2507 under equivalent operating conditions, with low relative overhead.

items.title: TCP options
items.text: Enhanced capabilities for compression of header fields, including TCP options such as SACK and Timestamp.

items.title: Fit the framework
items.text: Incorporation of TCP compression into the ROHC framework, alongside the other ROHC profiles.

viz.caption: THE HEADERS THE SCHEME HAS TO HANDLE

cells: All expected changes in the IP header fields, with IPv6 extensions present, and the ECN bits in use
The kinds of headers used by Mobile IPv4 and IPv6, including tunneled packets, the Routing Header and the Home Address Option
Headers containing IPsec subheaders where the NULL encryption algorithm is used. The encrypted part of an ESP header and the cryptographic data in an AH header cannot be compressed.
All fields supported by RFC 2507, and the cases when the SYN, FIN or TCP ECN bits are set
Any TCP option present, even if the option itself is not compressed. SACK and Timestamp should also be compressed.

items.title: Low relative overhead
items.text: The average header overhead relative to the payload, counting any auxiliary control or feedback channels the scheme uses.

items.title: No loss propagation
items.text: A loss between the compressor and the decompressor must not lose subsequent packets, and must not damage the context so that later headers decompress wrongly.

items.title: Leave the checksum alone
items.text: Residual errors may be saved in the context state, so the TCP checksum must be carried unmodified in all compressed headers, and TCP's own error detection must not be affected.

items.title: Cheap short connections
items.text: Mechanisms for efficient compression of short-lived TCP transfers, minimizing the size of context initiation headers.

items.title: Handle reordering
items.text: Moderate misordering, of 2 to 3 packets, should be handled efficiently, and larger misordering must at least be handled correctly.

items.title: No added delay
items.text: The scheme should not contribute significantly to the system delay budget.
